The default `maxAge` is **172,800,000 ms, which is 2 days**. If a cached copy is newer than that, Firecrawl returns it right away. Otherwise it scrapes fresh and updates the cache. Setting `maxAge: 0` bypasses the cache and always scrapes fresh.

This comes from the Fast Scraping page: https://docs.firecrawl.dev/features/fast-scraping

The v2 scrape API reference (https://docs.firecrawl.dev/api-reference/endpoint/scrape) says something different: "Default maxAge is extended to 2 years so existing cached pages remain eligible." I only saw that one search excerpt, not the full parameter table. So the docs disagree, or the API reference describes a newer change that the Fast Scraping page hasn't caught up with. If it matters for your use, set `maxAge` explicitly instead of relying on the default.

Firecrawl's Hobby plan includes **5,000 credits per month**. It costs $19/month billed monthly, or $16/month billed annually. Both [firecrawl.dev/pricing](https://www.firecrawl.dev/pricing) and the [billing docs](https://docs.firecrawl.dev/billing) list this figure.

The default `maxAge` is **172800000 ms, which is 2 days**. If a cached copy of the page is newer than that, Firecrawl returns it right away. If not, it scrapes the page fresh and caches the result.

Other points from the same section of the docs:
- Setting `maxAge` to `0` skips the cache, so every request does a full scrape. That is slower and more likely to fail.
- Cached results still cost 1 credit per page.
- Requests that use `changeTracking` bypass the cache, so `maxAge` is ignored.

Source: https://docs.firecrawl.dev/features/scrape#caching-and-maxage
